KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, Florida (CNN) -- So, what's harder, steering a space shuttle or out-machoing Tom Cruise on the set of "Top Gun"? Scott Altman is commander of the current space shuttle mission to upgrade the Hubble Space Telescope. Scott Altman laughs when he answers the question. "Flying a space shuttle is a little more challenging than what we did in the movie, although the flying was a lot of fun," said Altman, who knows more than a little about both. The retired Navy F-14 fighter pilot is the commander of the current space shuttle Atlantis mission to repair and upgrade the Hubble Space Telescope. He also doubled for the actors, including Cruise, during the Southern California shoot of the 1986 hit movie. Then a young pilot, Altman had just gotten back from a 7½-month tour onboard an aircraft carrier when he got the "Top Gun" call from his commanding officer. "The skipper of our squadron picked four guys he thought he could trust to have this kind of carte blanche to break the rules a little bit," Altman said. That included a scene in which a brazen Navy pilot buzzes the base's control tower. That would never happen in real life, Altman said. The movie features Cruise as a young naval aviator, Pete "Maverick" Mitchell, selected to attend fighter-pilot training school at the then-Miramar Naval Station north of San Diego. To prepare for the film, Cruise flew in the backseat of an F-14 several times, including once with Altman. "The actors were all pretty easy to get along with. Tom Cruise, for example, was very motivated," recalled Altman, who is making his fourth trip into space this week. "He enjoyed flying. He listened to what we told him and became a pilot himself after that." Altman is not one to brag about his flying in "Top Gun." The U.S. space agency, NASA, doesn't mention his film heroics, either. But Altman is in one of the movie's most memorable scenes. While flying upside down, inverted, Altman gives an obscene gesture to the pilot of an enemy plane. "They said go ahead and gesture at the other airplane," said Altman, 49, with a smile. "So when you're looking at the scene where he's communicating with the Russian, or the bad-guy pilots in the movie, that would be my finger." But the flying scenes with the actors didn't all work out as director Tony Scott had hoped. "The director had to pay $7,600 an hour to rent an airplane," Altman recalled. "But after a week of spending that much money on the airplanes, he decided he couldn't use the footage. The actors all looked a little green, he said." Altman and the other pilots earned $23 a day for their trouble. But his biggest disappointment was not getting to see the film as soon as it was released. He and the other pilots were invited to a preview screening, but a commanding officer would not let them go. And by the time the movie hit theaters, Altman was busy. He was overseas, on another seven-month tour of duty.

**From ‘Top Gun’ to the top of NASA: How Scott Altman went from Hollywood dogfights to saving Hubble**

Before Scott “Scooter” Altman commanded a space shuttle mission to one of the most famous scientific instruments ever built, he helped make one of Hollywood’s most famous flying movies look real.

Altman, a retired U.S. Navy captain, test pilot and NASA astronaut, occupies a rare crossover lane between pop culture and space history: He was among the elite Navy aviators who flew aerial sequences for the 1986 blockbuster **“Top Gun,”** then later became a shuttle commander on **Atlantis** for a daring mission to upgrade and repair the **Hubble Space Telescope**.

It is a résumé that sounds almost engineered for the movies: F-14 Tomcats, carrier aviation, astronaut selection, shuttle launches — and a high-stakes service call to a telescope orbiting hundreds of miles above Earth.

But Altman’s story is also a reminder that some of cinema’s most thrilling images and science’s most consequential missions depend on the same thing: people who can perform under pressure when there is no room for error.

## The real flying behind “Top Gun”

When “Top Gun” turned Navy fighter pilots into pop-culture icons, much of the film’s adrenaline came from real aircraft flown by real aviators. Altman, then a Navy F-14 pilot, was one of the pilots involved in the movie’s aerial work.

Long before computer-generated dogfights became standard blockbuster language, “Top Gun” relied heavily on practical flying — Tomcats banking, climbing and roaring across the sky in ways that helped define the film’s visual identity.

Altman’s role has become part of the lore surrounding the movie: a real Navy pilot helping bring fictional fighter ace Pete “Maverick” Mitchell’s world to life. The work required precision, coordination and a willingness to fly demanding profiles again and again for the camera.

It also required a quality that would later serve Altman in orbit: trust. In film flying, as in spaceflight, choreography is not optional. Every maneuver has to be planned, briefed and executed with discipline, because the margin between spectacle and danger can be thin.

## From fighter jets to space shuttle cockpits

Altman went on to become a NASA astronaut in the mid-1990s, trading the cockpit of a Tomcat for the flight deck of the space shuttle. He flew multiple shuttle missions, including as pilot and later as commander.

His career culminated in one of NASA’s most dramatic late-shuttle-era flights: **STS-125**, launched in May 2009 aboard **space shuttle Atlantis**.

The target was Hubble, the orbiting observatory that had transformed modern astronomy with images of galaxies, nebulae and deep fields that showed the universe in staggering detail. By 2009, Hubble needed help. Some instruments had failed or degraded. Critical systems required replacement. NASA planned one final servicing mission to extend the telescope’s life and sharpen its vision.

Altman commanded Atlantis on that mission.

Unlike shuttle flights to the International Space Station, a Hubble servicing mission had no safe harbor. Atlantis could not simply dock at the station if something went wrong; Hubble flies in a different orbit. That made STS-125 especially complex, and NASA prepared a rescue shuttle as a contingency.

The stakes were high: Send astronauts to repair Hubble in orbit, or risk losing one of humanity’s most productive scientific instruments.

## Atlantis meets Hubble

After launch, Atlantis caught up with Hubble and used the shuttle’s robotic arm to capture the telescope. What followed was a series of intricate spacewalks by the crew to replace, repair and upgrade key components.

The astronauts installed new instruments, including the **Wide Field Camera 3**, which would become one of Hubble’s most important tools, and the **Cosmic Origins Spectrograph**, designed to study the large-scale structure of the universe and the composition of intergalactic matter.

They also repaired instruments that were never designed to be fixed in space, replaced gyroscopes and batteries, and gave Hubble the tools it needed to keep operating well beyond its expected lifetime.

For Altman, commanding the mission meant overseeing a ballet of orbital mechanics, robotics, spacewalking and shuttle operations — a far cry from Hollywood, but not entirely unrelated. Both worlds demanded technical mastery. Both depended on timing. Both produced images that would outlast the moment.

## A telescope reborn

The success of STS-125 helped Hubble continue making discoveries for years. After the servicing mission, the telescope delivered new views of star-forming regions, distant galaxies, planets in our own solar system and the deep universe.

Hubble’s post-2009 science helped bridge the era between the shuttle program and newer observatories such as the James Webb Space Telescope. Many of the telescope’s most beloved images came after astronauts aboard Atlantis gave it new life.

Altman’s mission, in that sense, was not just a repair job. It was an act of preservation — keeping one of NASA’s most iconic spacecraft alive long enough to continue reshaping how humans see the cosmos.

## The Maverick-to-Hubble arc

Altman’s unusual connection to “Top Gun” gives his NASA career a cinematic frame, but the real story is bigger than a movie credit. It is about the continuum between aviation and spaceflight: the test pilots, engineers, astronauts and crews who move from high-performance aircraft to spacecraft, bringing a culture of precision with them.

In “Top Gun,” the drama was speed, rivalry and danger at low altitude. On Atlantis, the drama unfolded silently in orbit, with Earth turning below and Hubble locked in the shuttle’s payload bay.

One helped define the look of a generation’s favorite fighter-pilot fantasy. The other helped extend the life of a telescope that revealed the universe with unprecedented clarity.

Scott Altman did both.
